title: Poor proxies for leadership expertise
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart applies Rob Coe's poor proxies for learning to school leaders, arguing that learning is learning whether children or adults do it. Leadership expertise depends on domain-specific knowledge and its application, but it is as invisible as pupil learning, so we reach for proxies that mislead. He names four poor ones: leaders being busy, producing lots of documentation, running staff meetings and CPD, and having happy staff. Each can accompany expertise but none proves it. He then proposes better indicators drawn from how expertise actually develops: gathering informal knowledge of how persistent problems appear in your own school, building formal knowledge of curriculum, culture, teaching and behaviour, retrieving earlier thinking over time, and debriefing decisions with other leaders. He ends by cautioning that even these remain only proxies for what is hard to see.
points: Busyness, paperwork, running meetings and a content staff are poor proxies because they can all exist without leadership expertise.
Intention matters more than method: seeking out informal knowledge of your school's persistent problems builds expertise however you do it.
Leaders have a moral imperative to keep building formal knowledge of curriculum, culture, teaching and behaviour because knowledge determines decision quality.
Expertise grows when leaders retrieve earlier thinking after days, weeks and months rather than treating each decision as new.
Structured debriefs of past decisions, asking what was known and what options existed, build a better mental model for the next one.
quotes: Perhaps stronger is the need to answer to others for accountability purposes. Proxies exist to help make a judgement of whether learning is happening but many are poor
And there are many more but busy leaders are not necessarily expert leaders. These activities might well bring value but they are not an indicator of expertise.

A staffing body could be happy without these conditions though. They might be happy because they are completely left alone or there are lower expectations of them, which of course would not be symptomatic of leadership expertise.

When leaders deliberately seek out informal knowledge of their own school context, no matter how they do it, this contributes to their expertise. It is the intention that is important, not the means of finding out.
Leaders could spend all day observing what happen in lessons without seeing what’s happening and understanding why.

It is a moral imperative of leaders to keep building their formal knowledge of the core business of schools. What we know determines the quality of our decision making and undoubtedly, the most expert leaders make better decisions.

Engaging in discussion around past decisions helps us to build our knowledge of that situation and equip us with a better mental model. Leadership learning is like any other learning in both how it happens and how difficult it is to see.
